Beállítom „A magyar állam nevében ezennel felszólítom Mészáros Lőrincet és az MBH Bankot, hogy haladéktalanul vonja vissza a mélyszegénységben élő, kiváló tanulókat támogató program finanszírozását megszüntető döntését” – írta Facebook-oldalán Magyar Péter , miután a Telex megírta, hogy az MBH Bank 32 év után megszüntette a Nemzetközi Gyermekmentő Szolgálat ösztöndíjprogramjának finanszírozását . A bank a Telex kérdésére azt írta, már tavaly tájékoztatták erről a szándékukról a szervezetet, és egy év haladékot is adtak nekik, így volt lehetőségük felkészülni a változásra. Azt írták, a bank a 2023-as megalakulásakor a jogelőd intézményektől szerteágazó támogatási és szponzorációs portfóliót örökölt, amelyet felülvizsgált, és egy komplexebb társadalmi felzárkóztatási stratégiát fogadott el új stratégiai partnerségekre alapozva. Mindeközben fokozatosan lépett ki több lejáró együttműködésből, az NSZGY-t pedig már tavaly tájékoztatták arról, hogy az új stratégia alapján a lejáró, régebbi támogatási szerződést nem kívánják meghosszabbítani. A hírre reagálva Magyar Péter azt írta, „a harmincmilliárdos yachton ringatózó Mészáros Lőrinchez köthető MBH Bank 32 év után megszünteti száz, mélyszegénységben élő, kiválóan tanuló gyermekeket támogató ösztöndíjprogram finanszírozását. […] Az MBH Bank eközben százmilliárd forintot meghaladó összegért épít átláthatatlan módon luxuszékházat.” A miniszterelnök azt írta, a magyar állam az MBH Bank résztulajdonosa, ezért a magyar állam nevében felszólítja a bankot, hogy vonja vissza a döntését, és „azonnal hozza nyilvánosságra a bank százmilliárdos székházépítésének részleteit”. Az NGYSZ azt írta, a pénzintézet segítségével eddig minden évben 100 mélyszegénységben élő gyereknek adtak lehetőséget arra, hogy továbbtanuljanak. Egy gyermek egyéves támogatása 800 ezer forintba került. A bank tájékoztatása szerint évente több tízmillió forinttal támogatták a Nemzetközi Gyermekmentő Szolgálat munkáját. A szervezet azt írta, más szponzorok segítségével további 60 gyereknek a jövőben is biztosítja az ösztöndíját, és reméli, hogy új támogatók segítségével a kieső 100 gyerek támogatása is folytatódhat. Magyar Péter felszólításával kapcsolatban kerestük az MBH Bankot, amint választ kapunk, beszámolunk róla. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian History books Obituary Theodore Zeldin obituary Revered historian, author and francophile with a novelistic approach to his subject Stuart Jeffries Wed 18 Nov 2026 10.42 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 12.24 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On the website the Oxford Muse , which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.” During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. That is also what conversation seeks.” These reflections were typical of the way in which Zeldin, who has died aged 93, approached the past, transcended academic constraints and hoped for a better human future. “What is missing from the world is a sense of direction, because we are overwhelmed by the conflicts which surround us, as though we are marching through a jungle which never ends,” he wrote in the book Conversation (1998). “I should like some of us to start conversation to dispel that darkness … to create equality, to open ourselves to strangers, and most practically, to remake our working world, so that we are no longer isolated by our jargon or our professional boredom.” View image in fullscreen On his 75th birthday, in 2008, Zeldin initiated what he called “a feast of strangers”. Instead of inviting friends to celebrate at his art deco home outside Oxford, he issued an invitation through the media to everybody he did not know, to join him at an art gallery to have a conversation with a stranger. His aim was to get people to really understand one another by encouraging them to talk one-on-one for at least two hours about their priorities and the way they believe life should be conducted. “I’m constantly astounded by the way people talk so openly to someone they don’t know,” he told an interviewer. “They clarify in their own minds what is important to them, discover another person has similar problems, and create trust and even a friendship.” At a time when social theorists were inclined to academic obscurantism and/or Spenglerian gloom, Zeldin was an optimist. In An Intimate History of Humanity (1994), he wrote: “It is in the power of everybody, with a little courage, to hold out a hand to someone different, to listen, to attempt to increase, by even a tiny amount, the quantity of kindness and humanity in the world.” Whether one finds that optimism mawkish or inspiring depends on one’s temperament, but his sincerity was undeniable. Theodore was born to Russian Jewish parents on Mount Carmel, in the pre-Israel British mandate in Palestine. His mother, Emma, was a dentist, and his father, Jacob, was an engineer and mathematician who, Zeldin said in an interview with the Independent, “joined the British colonial service and went round improving the empire”. A child prodigy, he could read by the age of three. His first school report said: “He bestrides the school like a colossus.” Zeldin wrote his first book aged 12. After attending a boarding school in Cairo, he continued his education at Aylesbury grammar school, Buckinghamshire. At 15, he went to what is now Birkbeck, University of London because, as he said: “It had no upper age limit and thus no lower one either, so I was at university with greyheads.” He graduated with a degree in history in 1951. He then studied modern history at Christ Church, Oxford, where he had a formative experience. “One of the most silent men I have known ended up committing suicide,” he recalled. Zeldin had been one of a handful of students invited to lunches given by the college’s philosophy tutor. “He brought us together for conversation, but hardly ever spoke himself. And yet there was a wonderful warmth radiating from him, a gentleness, a modesty, which somehow made us talk, shy and ignorant though we were.” One day, there was a note pinned to the tutor’s door warning visitors that he had turned on the gas and they would find him dead. Thereafter, Zeldin took the task of speaking well as a duty – “like playing music, it requires attention and knowledge and practice,” he observed. He remained in Oxford, first as a DPhil student and later as a fellow of St Antony’s College, where he developed the university’s postgraduate centre for international studies, and was its dean for 13 years. My method is to hold up a multitude of mirrors around the French, so that they may be seen simultaneously from different angles His home was England, but his passion was France . He wrote The Political System of Napoleon III (1958), co-edited (with Anne Troisier de Diaz) the journals of Napoleon’s prime minister Émile Ollivier (1961) and published a book of essays, Conflicts in French Society: Anticlericalism, Education and Morals in the 19th Century (1970). But it was his 2,000-page, five-volume History of French Passions (Ambition and Love, Intellect and Pride, Taste and Corruption, Anxiety and Hypocrisy, Politics and Anger), published between 1973 and 1977, that best expressed his idiosyncratic approach to history and earned him enduring adoration. “He understands us better than we know ourselves,” claimed Livres de France. Le Point magazine pronounced him “the most popular Englishman in France”. Policemen saluted him in the street; train conductors upgraded him from second class to first. Zeldin – who was made CBE in 2001 – was appointed to the Légion d’honneur in 2012. “My method is to hold up a multitude of mirrors around the French, so that they may be seen simultaneously from different angles,” he explained in the preface to Ambition and Love, the first volume. He told a Financial Times interviewer: “In that book I looked at every aspect of life. What does it mean to dance? What does it mean to commit a crime? What does it mean to be anxious? What does it mean to tell a joke? The great thing about the French is that they have thought about these subjects in a great variety of ways and are a very articulate people.” In 2007, he served on the Attali commission , tasked with suggesting reforms to revivify France to the then president Nicolas Sarkozy. Zeldin’s brief was to come up with ideas to “change mentalities”. Undaunted, he suggested – among other measures – that school teachers be posted to foreign countries for a year to experience different cultures. View image in fullscreen His kaleidoscopic, even novelistic approach to history – more Balzacian than Oxonian – served him well in later books, notably An Intimate History of Humanity, in which he interviewed people, mostly French and overwhelmingly female, about human needs and desires, ending up with chapters such as “How men and women have slowly learned to have interesting conversations” and “How people have freed themselves from fear by finding new fears”. He went from personal to epochal, trying to work out how concepts of personal fulfilment, sexual relations or family obligation have differed over time. And he encouraged us to change them again. He was impressed by those who have imagined how they might change the ends of their lives and then, courageously, cast off the presumed shackles of historical determinism, and thereby realised what they imagined. In his 1988 absurdist novel Happiness, a young woman called Sumdy visits Paradise on a roundtrip ticket and meets kamikaze pilots and Einstein. She returns chastened: happiness, it turns out, is an outdated idea rather than the summum bonum of human life. Such is the novel’s moral and Zeldin’s principal theme: our challenge is to imagine different ends and have the courage to pursue them. Happiness, for Zeldin, was not enough. In his later years Zeldin’s particular concern was to free people from demeaning work. As an associate fellow of the Saïd Business School in Oxford, and much in demand on the international lecture circuit, he once visited an Indian factory making electrical equipment, where he saw “rows and rows of Indian women fiddling around with bits and pieces”. The manager said he wanted to turn these employees into entrepreneurs. Zeldin replied that it would be impossible if they spent eight hours a day performing boring tasks. The manager agreed to mechanise some of their routine functions and devote two hours a day to educating his workers. “That’s the kind of revolution that interests me,” Zeldin said. In 1975 he married Deirdre Wilson, whom he met at Oxford when she was an undergraduate and who became emeritus professor of speech, hearing and phonetic sciences at University College London. Wilson became renowned for developing, with the French cognitive scientist Dan Sperber, relevance theory – an attempt to tackle the paradox of how human comprehension can ever be achieved since, as Wilson and Sperber put it in their 2012 book Meaning and Relevance, when people speak, their words never fully encode what they mean, and the context is always compatible with a variety of interpretations. Doubtless the focus of their research appealed to Zeldin’s sense of the importance of conversation and how, in practice, it works. He said of their marriage: “The fact that we have no children makes it easier for us to separate, but also brings us closer emotionally.” The essence of a relationship, Zeldin believed, is that it must every day seem worthwhile. In that, as in much else, he was an optimist who realised that the art of living requires work as well as virtuosity. He is survived by Deirdre.
